query_snapshot: According to NBS Circular 592, which molybdenum-bearing stainless-steel types were reported as most resistant to sulfuric acid at low temperatures, and what limitations prevent treating that statement as a universal material recommendation?
final_answer:
Evidence-grounded answer:

- NBS Circular 592 reports that molybdenum-bearing stainless steels types 316 and 317 "were the most resistant at low temperatures." [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485; nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- The Circular states that at about 150° F all of the stainless steels "corrode in practically all concentrations of acid from [corrupted lower-bound character] to 95 percent." [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485; nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- Roach and Hall reported that molybdenum-bearing stainless steels were useful, at room temperature, in concentrations of sulfuric acid below 15 percent and above 85 percent. [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485; nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- The Circular notes that resistance to sulfuric acid can be improved in some cases by additions of copper or cerium. [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485; nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- The Circular explains that halide ions and aeration/flow can attack the passive film and produce pitting; additions of molybdenum reduce susceptibility to pitting but do not remove other dependencies. [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485; nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
- The Circular identifies additional factors that limit generalization of the "most resistant" statement, including temperature, acid concentration, impurities/aeration, presence of halides, mechanical and residual stresses (stress‑corrosion cracking), welding/fabrication history (residual flux, carbide or sigma‑phase precipitation), and other metallurgical or service conditions. [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485; nbscircular592.pdf, p. 60, chunk 2b809bc1]
